verses.text: There was a man named Job in the land of Uz. Job was blameless and upright. He feared God and stayed away from evil.
He had seven sons and three daughters.
He owned 7,000 sheep, 3,000 camels, 500 pairs of oxen, and 500 female donkeys. His household was huge. He was the greatest of all the people of the east.
Each of his sons hosted a feast at his own house on his birthday. They’d send for their three sisters to come eat and drink with them.

When the days of feasting were over, Job would send for them and set them apart as holy. He’d get up early and make a burnt offering for each of them. Job thought, “Maybe my sons sinned and turned their backs on God in their hearts.” He kept doing this every time.
One day God’s sons came to stand before the LORD, and Satan came along with them.
The LORD asked Satan, “Where have you been?” Satan answered, “Going back and forth across the earth, walking all over it.”
The LORD asked Satan, “Have you taken a look at my servant Job? There’s nobody like him on earth. He’s blameless and upright, he fears God, and he turns away from evil.”
Satan answered the LORD, “Does Job fear God for nothing?
Haven’t you put a hedge around him, his household, and everything he owns, on every side? You’ve blessed his work, and his possessions keep growing across the land.
But reach out your hand and touch everything he owns, and he’ll turn his back on you right to your face.”
The LORD told Satan, “All right, everything he owns is in your power. Just don’t lay a hand on Job himself.” So Satan left the LORD’s presence.
One day Job’s sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine at their oldest brother’s house.
A messenger came to Job and said, “The oxen were plowing, and the donkeys were feeding right beside them.
Then the Sabeans attacked and took the animals. They killed the servants with the sword. I’m the only one who got away to tell you.”
While he was still talking, another messenger came and said, “God’s fire fell from the sky and burned up the sheep and the servants. It consumed them all. I’m the only one who got away to tell you.”

While that one was still talking, another came and said, “The Chaldeans formed three groups and swept in on the camels. They took them and killed the servants with the sword. I’m the only one who got away to tell you.”
While that one was still talking, another came and said, “Your sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine at their oldest brother’s house.
Then a powerful wind came out of the wilderness and hit all four corners of the house. It collapsed on the young people, and they died. I’m the only one who got away to tell you.”
Job stood up, tore his robe, and shaved his head. Then he fell to the ground and worshiped.
He said, “I came naked from my mother’s womb, and naked I’ll return there. The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away. Praise the LORD’s name.”
Through all of this, Job didn’t sin or accuse God of doing wrong.
Another day, God’s sons came to stand before the LORD. Satan came along with them to stand before the LORD too.
The LORD asked Satan, “Where have you come from?” Satan answered, “I’ve been going back and forth across the earth, walking all over it.”

The LORD asked Satan, “Have you taken a look at my servant Job? There’s nobody like him on earth. He’s blameless and upright, he fears God, and he turns away from evil. He’s still holding on to his integrity, even though you stirred me up against him to ruin him for no reason.”
Satan answered the LORD, “Skin for skin. A person will give up everything they own to stay alive.
But reach out your hand and touch his bones and flesh, and he’ll turn his back on you right to your face.”
The LORD told Satan, “All right, he’s in your hands. Just spare his life.”
So Satan left the LORD’s presence and struck Job with painful sores from the soles of his feet to the top of his head.
Job found a piece of broken pottery to scrape his skin with and sat there among the ashes.
His wife said, “Are you still holding on to your integrity? Turn your back on God and die.”
He told her, “You’re talking like one of the foolish women. What, should we take good from God’s hand and refuse trouble?” Through all this, Job didn’t sin in what he said.

When Job’s three friends heard about all the trouble that had come on him, they each came from home: Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite. They arranged to go together to share his grief and comfort him.
When they looked up from a distance, they didn’t recognize him. They cried out and wept. Each tore his robe and tossed dust over his head toward the sky.
They sat with him on the ground for seven days and seven nights. Nobody said a word to him, because they could see how deep his grief was.
After that, Job spoke up and cursed the day he was born.
Here’s what Job said:
“Let the day I was born disappear, and the night that said, ‘A boy has been conceived.’
Let that day go dark. May God above never look for it, and may no light shine on it.
Let darkness and the shadow of death claim it. Let a cloud settle over it. Let everything that blacks out the day make it tremble.
Let thick darkness grab hold of that night. May it never celebrate with the days of the year or be counted in any month.
Let that night be barren. May no shout of joy be heard in it.
Let those who curse the day curse that night, the ones ready to wake Leviathan.
Let its twilight stars go dark. Let it wait for light that never comes. May it never see dawn open its eyes,
because it didn’t close the doors of my mother’s womb or keep trouble out of my sight.
“Why didn’t I die as I came out of the womb? Why didn’t I breathe my last when my mother gave birth to me?
Why were there knees to hold me? Why was there a breast for me to nurse at?
By now I’d be lying still and quiet. I’d be asleep and at rest,
with the kings and advisers of the earth who rebuilt ruined places for themselves,
or with rulers who had gold and filled their houses with silver.
Or I’d never have lived at all, like a child lost before its time, like babies who never saw the light.
There the wicked stop causing trouble, and the worn-out finally rest.
There prisoners can sit together in peace. They don’t hear the taskmaster’s voice.
The small and the great are both there, and the servant is free from his master.
“Why give light to someone in misery, or life to people who are bitter inside,
who long for death that never comes, who dig for it harder than they’d dig for buried treasure,
who celebrate and rejoice when they find the grave?
Why give light to a man who can’t see his way forward, a man God has fenced in?
I sigh before I eat. My groans pour out like water.
The very thing I dread has come on me. What I was afraid of has found me.
I have no ease, no quiet, no rest. Trouble just keeps coming.”
Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered:
“If someone dares to say something to you, will it upset you? But who can keep quiet?
Look, you’ve taught many people and strengthened hands that had gone weak.
Your words held up people who were about to fall. You steadied knees that were giving way.
But now trouble’s come for you, and you’re worn out. It touches you, and you’re shaken.
Isn’t your reverence for God what gives you confidence? Isn’t the way you’ve lived with integrity what gives you hope?
“Think about it. Who ever died while innocent? Where were upright people ever cut down?
Here’s what I’ve seen: people who plow up wrongdoing and plant trouble harvest the same thing.
God’s breath wipes them out. A blast of his anger consumes them.
The lion’s roar, the fierce lion’s growl, and the young lions’ teeth are all broken.
The old lion dies for lack of prey, and the lioness’s cubs scatter.
“Something came to me in secret. I caught just a whisper of it.
As I thought about visions in the night, when people fall into deep sleep,
fear and trembling came over me. Every bone in my body shook.
A spirit passed in front of my face, and the hair on my body stood up.
It stopped, but I couldn’t make out what it looked like. A shape stood before my eyes. There was silence, and then I heard a voice:
‘Can a mortal be more just than God? Can a person be more pure than their Maker?
Look, God doesn’t put his trust in his servants. He finds fault even with his angels.
How much less can he trust those who live in houses of clay, with foundations in the dust, who are crushed before a moth!
Between morning and evening they’re destroyed. They’re gone for good, and nobody even notices.
Isn’t their tent cord pulled up from within them? They die without gaining wisdom.’”
“Go ahead, call out. Is anyone going to answer you? Which of the holy ones will you turn to?
Resentment kills a fool, and jealousy kills the naive.
I’ve seen a fool take root, but then I suddenly cursed the place he lived.
His children are nowhere near safe. They’re crushed at the gate, and nobody comes to rescue them.
Hungry people eat up his harvest and take it even from among the thorns. The snare stands open for everything they own.
Hardship doesn’t come out of the dust, and trouble doesn’t sprout from the ground.
People are born into trouble, as surely as sparks fly up.
“But if it were me, I’d seek God. I’d put my case in his hands.
He does great things we can’t wrap our heads around, more wonders than anyone can count.
He gives rain to the earth and sends water onto the fields.
He lifts up those who’ve been brought low and raises those who mourn to safety.
He wrecks the plans of crafty people so their hands can’t pull off what they planned.
He catches the wise in their own schemes, and the plans of the cunning come crashing down.
They run into darkness in broad daylight and feel their way around at noon like it’s the middle of the night.
But he rescues the needy from the sword of their words and from the grip of the powerful.
So the poor have hope, and injustice shuts its mouth.
“Look, how fortunate is the person God corrects! So don’t brush off the Almighty’s discipline.
He wounds, and he bandages the wound. He injures, and his own hands heal.
He’ll rescue you from six troubles. Even in seven, no harm will touch you.
In a famine, he’ll rescue you from death. In war, he’ll save you from the power of the sword.
You’ll be sheltered from the lash of people’s words. You won’t be scared when destruction comes.
You’ll laugh at destruction and famine, and you won’t be afraid of wild animals.
The stones of the field will be on your side, and the animals in the fields will be at peace with you.
You’ll know your tent is safe. You’ll check on your fold and find nothing missing.
You’ll know your descendants will be many, as plentiful as grass on the earth.
You’ll go to your grave at a ripe old age, like a bundle of grain brought in at the right time.
Look, we’ve looked into it, and this is how it is. Listen and take it to heart for your own good.”
Then Job answered:
“If only someone could weigh my anguish and pile all my misery onto the scales!
It would weigh more than the sand of the seas. That’s why I’ve spoken so rashly.
The Almighty’s arrows are lodged in me. My spirit drinks their poison. God’s terrors line up against me.
Does a wild donkey bray when it has grass? Does an ox bellow over its feed?
Can you eat something bland without salt? Does egg white have any taste?
I can’t bring myself to touch those things. To me they’re like food that makes me sick.
“If only I could get what I’ve asked for, if only God would give me what I’m longing for.
If only God would choose to crush me, let his hand loose, and cut me off!
Even in pain that gives me no break, I’d still have this comfort and could still rejoice: I haven’t denied the words of the Holy One.
How much strength do I have left to keep waiting? What’s ahead of me that I should keep being patient?
Am I as strong as stone? Is my skin made of bronze?
I’ve got no help left in me, and wisdom has been driven away from me, hasn’t it?
“A friend should show kindness to someone who’s about to give out, even if that person stops fearing the Almighty.
My brothers have let me down like a stream you can’t count on, like streambeds whose waters disappear.
They run dark with ice, and snow hides in them.
Come the dry season, they vanish. When the heat hits, they dry up right where they were.
Caravans following them turn aside, head into the wasteland, and die.
The caravans from Tema looked for them. The travelers from Sheba counted on them.
They came with so much confidence, but when they got there, they were shaken and let down.
Now you’re just like those streams, no help at all. You see something terrifying and get scared.
Did I ever say, ‘Give me something,’ or ‘Pay a gift for me out of your own wealth’?
Did I say, ‘Rescue me from my enemy’s grip,’ or ‘Buy me back from the hands of those who oppress me’?
“Teach me, and I’ll be quiet. Show me where I went wrong.
Honest words can hit hard. But what does your scolding actually prove wrong?
Are you trying to pick apart my words when what a desperate person says is like wind?
You’d even cast lots for an orphan and sell your own friend like goods.
Now please look at me. I won’t lie to your face.
Please think again. Don’t be unfair. Yes, take another look. My case is right.
Is there anything unjust on my tongue? Can’t I taste when something is wrong?”
“Isn’t life on earth a stint of hard labor? Aren’t our days like a hired worker’s?
A servant longs for shade, and a hired hand watches for payday.
That’s how I’ve been handed months of misery and nights that wear me out.
When I lie down, I think, ‘When can I get up? When will this night be over?’ I toss and turn till dawn.
My body is covered with worms and clumps of dirt. My skin closes up, then breaks open again.
My days fly faster than a weaver’s shuttle, and they run out without hope.
Remember, my life is just a breath. My eyes won’t see good again.
Those who see me now won’t see me anymore. You’ll look for me, but I’ll be gone.
A cloud fades and disappears. In the same way, whoever goes down to Sheol won’t come back up.
They won’t go home again. Even their own place won’t know them anymore.
“So I’m done keeping quiet. I’ll speak out of the anguish in my spirit. I’ll tell you how bitter I feel inside.
Am I the sea or a sea monster? Is that why you’ve put a guard on me?
When I think, ‘My bed will comfort me. Lying down will ease my pain,’
you scare me with dreams and terrify me with visions.
That’s why I’d choose strangling, even death, over living in this body.
I can’t stand my life. I don’t want to live forever. Leave me alone. My days are barely a breath.
What are human beings that you make so much of them and pay them so much attention?
Why check on them every morning and test them every moment?
How long before you look away and give me enough time to swallow my own spit?
If I’ve sinned, what have I done to you, watcher of humanity? Why make me your target until I’m a burden to myself?
Why won’t you forgive my disobedience and take away my wrong? Soon I’ll lie down in the dust. You’ll search hard for me, but I’ll be gone.”
Then Bildad the Shuhite answered:
“How long are you going to talk like this? Are the words coming out of your mouth going to be one big gust of wind?
Does God twist justice? Does the Almighty twist what’s right?
If your children sinned against him, he handed them over to the consequences of their disobedience.
If you’re going to seek God earnestly, bring your plea to the Almighty.
If you’re pure and upright, surely he’ll rise to act for you now and make your home thrive again, where you’ve lived uprightly.
Your beginning may have been small, but what comes later will be far greater.
“Go ask the generations before us. Find out what their ancestors learned.
We only got here yesterday, and we know nothing. Our days on earth are just a shadow.
Won’t they teach you and tell you what they know? Won’t they speak from the heart?
“Can papyrus grow without mud? Can rushes grow without water?
While still green, before anyone cuts it down, it dries up faster than any other reed.
That’s how it goes for everyone who forgets God. The hope of a godless person dies out.
What they count on breaks apart. What they trust is a spider’s web.
They lean on their house, but it won’t stand. They grab hold of it, but it won’t hold up.
They’re like a green plant in the sun, sending shoots all through the garden.
Its roots wrap around the pile of rocks and reach the place full of stones.
If it’s torn out of its spot, that very place will deny it, saying, ‘Never seen you before.’
Look, that’s the joy of its life. Others will spring up from the soil.
“Look, God won’t throw away someone who’s blameless, and he won’t lend evildoers a hand.
He’ll still fill your mouth with laughter and put shouts of joy on your lips.
The people who hate you will wear their shame, and the tent of the wicked will be gone.”
Then Job answered:
“I know that’s true. But how can a person be in the right before God?
If someone wanted to argue a case with him, they couldn’t answer him even once in a thousand times.
God is wise at heart and mighty in strength. Who’s ever dug in against him and come out ahead?
He moves mountains before they know what hit them. He flips them over in his anger.
He shakes the earth out of its place, and its pillars tremble.
He tells the sun to stay down, and it doesn’t rise. He seals up the stars.
He alone stretches out the heavens and walks on the waves of the sea.
He made the Bear, Orion, the Pleiades, and the chambers of the south.
He does great things we can’t figure out, more wonders than anyone can count.
Look, he goes right past me, and I don’t see him. He moves on, and I don’t even sense him.
Look, he snatches things away. Who can stop him? Who’ll ask him, ‘What are you doing?’
“God won’t pull back his anger. Even Rahab’s helpers bow down beneath him.
So how could I answer him? How could I find the words to argue my case with him?
Even if I were in the right, I wouldn’t answer back. I’d plead with my judge.
Even if I called and he answered, I still wouldn’t believe he’d listened to my voice.
He breaks me with a storm and piles wound upon wound for no reason.
He won’t let me catch my breath. He fills me with bitterness.
If it’s about strength, look how mighty he is! If it’s about justice, he says, ‘Who’s going to summon me?’
Even if I’m in the right, my own mouth will condemn me. Even if I’m blameless, it’ll make me out to be crooked.
I’m blameless. I don’t care about myself. I can’t stand my life.
“It all comes to the same thing. That’s why I say he destroys both the blameless and the wicked.
When a scourge kills suddenly, he mocks what innocent people are going through.
The earth is handed over to the wicked. He covers the eyes of its judges. If it isn’t him, then who is it?
“My days are faster than a runner now. They fly by without seeing anything good.
They’ve swept past like fast ships, like an eagle swooping on its prey.
If I think, ‘I’ll forget my complaint, wipe the sadness off my face, and cheer up,’
I’m still scared of all my sorrows. I know you won’t hold me innocent.
I’m going to be condemned anyway. Why wear myself out for nothing?
Even if I wash myself with snow and scrub my hands clean with lye,
you’ll still throw me into a ditch. Even my own clothes will be disgusted with me.
He isn’t human like I am, so I can’t answer him or take him to court.
There’s no one to settle things between us, no one who can lay a hand on both of us.
Let him take his rod away from me and stop terrifying me.
Then I’d speak without being afraid of him, because that fear isn’t who I am inside.”
“I’m worn out with my life. I’m going to let my complaint out and speak from the bitterness deep inside me.
I’ll tell God, ‘Don’t condemn me. Show me why you’re taking up a case against me.
Does it please you to crush me, look down on what your own hands made, and smile on the plans of the wicked?
Do you have eyes made of flesh? Do you see things the way people do?
Are your days like a mortal’s days, or your years like a person’s years,
that you have to dig for my wrongdoing and search for my sin?
You know I’m not wicked, and there’s nobody who can rescue me from your hand.
“‘Your hands shaped every part of me, and now you’re tearing me down.
Please remember that you shaped me like clay. Are you going to turn me back into dust?
Didn’t you pour me out like milk and let me thicken like cheese?
You wrapped me in skin and flesh and knitted me together with bones and sinews.
You gave me life and showed me faithful love. Your care kept my spirit alive.
Yet you kept these things hidden in your heart. I know this is what you had in mind:
If I sin, you’ll take note of it, and you won’t clear me of what I’ve done.
If I’m wicked, I’m in for trouble. Even if I’m in the right, I still can’t lift my head. I’m full of shame and painfully aware of what I’m suffering.
If I lift my head, you hunt me like a lion. You show me your power all over again.
You bring fresh witnesses against me, and your anger at me keeps growing. Wave after wave of battle comes against me.
“‘So why did you bring me out of the womb? I wish I’d breathed my last before anyone saw me.
It would’ve been as if I’d never existed. I would’ve been carried straight from the womb to the grave.
Haven’t I got just a few days left? Stop and leave me alone so I can find a little comfort,
before I go to the place I’ll never come back from, the land of darkness and the shadow of death,
a land as dark as midnight, where the shadow of death hangs over everything, where nothing is in order and even the light is like midnight.’”
Then Zophar the Naamathite answered:
“Should all those words go unanswered? Does talking a lot make a person right?
Do you think your bragging will shut everyone up? When you mock, won’t anyone call you out and put you to shame?
You say, ‘What I teach is pure. I’m clean in your eyes.’
If only God would speak up and answer you himself!
If only he’d show you wisdom’s secrets! True wisdom has more than one side. Get this: God is asking less of you than your wrongdoing deserves.
“Can you get to the bottom of God’s mystery? Can you find the limits of the Almighty?
They’re as high as heaven. What can you do? They’re deeper than Sheol. What can you know?
Their measure stretches farther than the earth and wider than the sea.
If he comes by, locks someone up, or calls a court to order, who can stand against him?
He knows who’s deceitful. He sees wrongdoing without having to stop and study it.
An empty-headed person will get wise when a human is born as a wild donkey’s colt.
“If you set your heart right, reach out your hands to him.
If there’s wrongdoing in your hands, get it far away from you. Don’t let wrong take up residence in your tents.
Then you’ll lift your face without a stain. You’ll stand firm, and you won’t be afraid.
You’ll forget your misery and remember it like water that’s already flowed past.
Life will be brighter than noon. Even the darkness will be like morning.
You’ll feel secure because there’s hope. You’ll look around and be able to rest in safety.
You’ll lie down, and no one will scare you. Many people will come looking for your favor.
But the eyes of the wicked will fail. They’ll have nowhere to run. Their hope will be to breathe their last.”
Then Job answered:
“Of course, you’re the only people who know anything. When you die, I guess wisdom dies with you.
But I can think just as well as you can. I’m no less than you. Who doesn’t already know these things?
I’ve become the joke of my neighbors, me, the one who called on God and got an answer. A person can be just and blameless and still be the joke.
People who have it easy look down on trouble. They have contempt ready for anyone whose foot slips.
Robbers’ tents thrive. Those who provoke God live in safety, carrying their god in their own hands.
“But go ask the animals. They’ll teach you. Ask the birds in the sky. They’ll tell you.
Talk to the earth, and it’ll teach you. The fish in the sea will tell you too.
Who among all these doesn’t know that the LORD’s hand has done this?
In his hand is the life of every living thing and the breath of every human being.
Doesn’t the ear test words the way your mouth tastes food?
Wisdom comes with age, and understanding with many years.
“God has wisdom and strength. He knows what to do and understands what’s going on.
Look, when he tears something down, nobody can build it back up. When he locks someone up, nobody can let them out.
When he holds back the waters, they dry up. When he sends them out, they overturn the land.
Strength and wisdom are his. Both the one who gets fooled and the one who fools them are his.
He leads advisers away stripped and turns judges into fools.
He undoes the bonds of kings and ties a belt around their waists.
He leads priests away stripped and brings down the mighty.
He takes the words away from people everyone trusts and strips the elders of their understanding.
He pours contempt on rulers and loosens the belts of the strong.
He brings hidden things up out of darkness and brings the shadow of death into the light.
He makes nations grow, and he destroys them. He makes nations spread, and he leads them away captive.
He takes away the understanding of the earth’s leaders and leaves them wandering in a wilderness with no path.
They feel their way through the dark without a light. He makes them stagger like someone who’s drunk.”
“Look, I’ve seen all this with my own eyes. I’ve heard it and understood it.
What you know, I know too. I’m every bit your equal.
“I want to speak to the Almighty himself. I want to argue my case with God.
But you make up lies. Every one of you is a doctor who can’t do a thing for me.
If only you’d go completely quiet! That would be the wise thing to do.
Hear me out now. Listen to the case I’m making.
Are you going to say unjust things for God? Are you going to lie on his behalf?
Are you going to play favorites and take God’s side? Are you going to argue his case for him?
Would it go well for you if he looked closely at you? Can you fool him the way you fool a person?
He’ll call you out if you secretly play favorites.
Won’t his majesty scare you? Won’t dread of him come over you?
Your clever sayings are proverbs made of ashes. Your defenses are made of clay.
“Quiet! Leave me alone so I can speak. Whatever happens to me, let it happen.
Why should I take my flesh in my teeth and put my life in my own hands?
Look, he’ll kill me. I have no hope. Still, I’ll defend the way I’ve lived right in front of him.
This too will be my salvation: a godless person wouldn’t come before him.
Listen closely to what I’m saying. Let my statement reach your ears.
Look, I’ve got my case in order. I know I’m in the right.
Who’s going to argue against me? If someone could, I’d go quiet and breathe my last.
“Just don’t do these two things to me, and I won’t hide from your face:
Take your hand far away from me, and don’t let your terror make me afraid.
Then call me and I’ll answer. Or let me speak and you answer me.
How many wrongs and sins have I committed? Show me my disobedience and my sin.
Why hide your face and treat me like your enemy?
Are you going to harass a leaf blowing in the wind? Are you going to chase dry stubble?
You write bitter charges against me and make me answer for the wrongs I did when I was young.
You put my feet in stocks, watch every path I take, and set a boundary for the soles of my feet,
even though I’m wasting away like something rotten, like clothes eaten by moths.
“A person born of a woman has only a few days, and they’re full of trouble.
They spring up like a flower and get cut down. They slip away like a shadow and don’t last.
Do you really watch someone like that so closely? Do you really bring me before you for judgment?
Who can bring something clean out of something unclean? Nobody.
You’ve already set the number of a person’s days. You know how many months they have, and you’ve set a limit they can’t cross.
Look away from them and let them rest, until they’ve finished their day like a hired worker.
“A tree still has hope. Cut it down, and it can sprout again. Its young shoots won’t give out.
Its roots may grow old in the earth, and its stump may die in the ground,
but at the scent of water it’ll bud and put out branches like a young plant.
But a person dies and is laid low. They breathe their last, and where are they?
As water disappears from the sea and a river dwindles and dries up,
so a person lies down and doesn’t get up. Until the heavens are gone, they won’t wake or be stirred out of their sleep.
“If only you’d hide me in Sheol and keep me out of sight until your anger passed! If only you’d set a time and remember me!
If someone dies, will they live again? I’d wait through every day of my struggle until my release came.
You’d call, and I’d answer you. You’d long for what your own hands made.
But now you count my steps. Aren’t you keeping watch over my sin?
You’ve sealed my disobedience in a bag. You’ve tied up my wrongdoing.
“But even a mountain falls and crumbles. A rock gets knocked out of its place.
Water wears down stones. Floods wash away the soil. That’s how you wear away a person’s hope.
You overpower them for good, and they’re gone. You change their face and send them away.
Their sons rise to honor, and they don’t know it. Their sons are brought low, and they don’t realize what’s happened to them.
Their own body hurts, and deep inside they mourn.”
Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered:
“Would a wise person answer with empty knowledge and fill up on the east wind?
Would they argue with useless talk or make speeches that do no good?
You’re doing away with reverence and getting in the way of devotion to God.
Your wrongdoing tells your mouth what to say, and you choose the words of crafty people.
Your own mouth condemns you. I don’t have to. Your own lips testify against you.
“Were you the first human ever born? Were you brought forth before the hills?
Did you hear God’s private counsel? Do you think you have all the wisdom to yourself?
What do you know that we don’t? What do you understand that we haven’t grasped?
We’ve got gray-haired people and elders on our side, people much older than your father.
Is the comfort God offers too little for you? What about the words spoken gently to you?
Why do you let your heart carry you away? Why do your eyes flash like that,
so that you turn your spirit against God and let those words come out of your mouth?
What is a human being, that they could be clean? How could anyone born of a woman be righteous?
Look, God doesn’t even put his trust in his holy ones. Even the heavens aren’t clean in his sight.
So how much less the vile and corrupt person who drinks wrongdoing like water!
“I’ll show you. Hear me out. I’ll tell you what I’ve seen,
what wise people learned from their ancestors and passed on without hiding it.
The land was given to them alone, and no outsider passed among them.
The wicked person twists in pain all their days, through all the years set aside for the oppressor.
Terrifying sounds ring in their ears. Even when things are going well, the destroyer comes for them.
They don’t believe they’ll make it back out of the darkness. The sword is waiting for them.
They roam around looking for bread, saying, ‘Where is it?’ They know the day of darkness is close at hand.
Distress and anguish scare them and overpower them like a king ready for battle.
That’s because they’ve raised their hand against God and acted arrogantly toward the Almighty.
They charge at him, stiff-necked, behind the thick parts of their shields,
because they’ve grown fat in the face and piled up fat on their thighs.
They’ve lived in ruined towns, in houses nobody lived in, places about to crumble into heaps.
They won’t get rich. Their wealth won’t last, and their possessions won’t spread across the land.
They won’t escape the darkness. A flame will dry out their branches, and the breath of God’s mouth will sweep them away.
Let them stop fooling themselves by trusting in emptiness, because emptiness is what they’ll get in return.
It’ll happen before their time, and their branch won’t stay green.
They’ll drop their unripe grapes like a vine and shed their blossoms like an olive tree.
The company of the godless will be barren, and fire will burn up the tents of those who take bribes.
They conceive trouble and give birth to wrongdoing. In their hearts they get deceit ready.”
Then Job answered:
“I’ve heard plenty of talk like that. Every one of you is awful at comforting people!
Will this empty talk ever end? What’s got you so worked up that you have to answer?
I could talk just like you if we traded places. I could string words together against you and shake my head at you.
But I’d use my words to give you strength. What I said would ease your pain.
“Even when I speak, my grief doesn’t let up. And if I stay quiet, what relief do I get?
Now, God, you’ve worn me out. You’ve left everyone around me desolate.
You’ve shriveled me up, and that stands as a witness against me. My wasted body gets up and testifies right to my face.
In his anger he’s torn me apart and pursued me. He’s gnashed his teeth at me. My enemy fixes a sharp stare on me.
They gape at me with open mouths. They slap my cheek to shame me. They all gang up on me.
God hands me over to the godless and throws me into the grip of the wicked.
I was at ease, and he broke me apart. He grabbed me by the neck and smashed me to pieces. Then he set me up as his target.
His archers surround me. He splits open my kidneys without holding back. He spills my bile onto the ground.
He breaks through me again and again. He charges at me like a giant.
I’ve sewn sackcloth onto my skin and shoved my horn into the dust.
My face is red from crying, and deep darkness hangs over my eyelids,
even though my hands have done no violence and my prayer is pure.
“Earth, don’t cover up my blood. Let my cry never find a place to rest.
Look, even now my witness is in heaven. The one who vouches for me is on high.
My friends mock me. My eyes pour out tears to God,
that he would uphold a person’s rights before God, as one person would for a neighbor!
In just a few years, I’ll go down the road I can’t come back from.
“My spirit is worn out. My days have burned out, and the grave is ready for me.
I’m surrounded by people who mock me. I can’t look away from the way they provoke me.
“Put up a pledge for me. Be my guarantor before yourself. Who else will shake hands on my behalf?
You’ve kept their hearts from understanding, so you won’t lift them up.
If someone turns in their friends for a share of the plunder, even their children’s eyes will fail.
“But he’s made my name a byword among the people. They spit in my face.
My eyes have gone dim with grief. My whole body is barely a shadow.
Upright people will be stunned at this. The innocent will rise up against the godless.
Still, those who are righteous will stick to their path, and those with clean hands will grow stronger and stronger.
But come on back, all of you. I won’t find a single wise person among you.
My days are gone. My plans are shattered, along with the hopes I held in my heart.
They turn night into day, saying, ‘The light is close,’ even with darkness right in front of them.
If I look to Sheol as my home and spread out my bed in the dark,
if I call decay ‘my father’ and say to the worm, ‘My mother, my sister,’
then where’s my hope? Who can even see it?
Will it go down with me to the gates of Sheol? Will we go down into the dust together?”
Then Bildad the Shuhite answered:
“How long are you going to keep hunting for words? Think it through first. Then we can talk.
Why do you count us as animals and see us as unclean?
You’re tearing yourself apart in anger. Should the earth be deserted for your sake? Should a rock be moved out of its place for you?
“Yes, the light of the wicked will go out. Not a spark from their fire will shine.
The light in their tent will go dark, and the lamp above them will go out.
Their once-powerful stride will get shorter, and their own plans will bring them down.
Their own feet will carry them into a net. They’ll walk straight into its mesh.
A snare will grab them by the heel. A trap will catch them.
A noose is hidden in the ground for them, and a trap is waiting on the path.
Terrors will scare them on every side and chase right at their heels.
Their strength will waste away, and disaster will be waiting right beside them.
Their body will be eaten away. Death’s firstborn will devour their limbs.
They’ll be ripped out of the safety of their tent and brought to the king of terrors.
What doesn’t belong to them will move into their tent. Sulfur will be scattered over their home.
Their roots will dry up below, and their branches will be cut off above.
Their memory will vanish from the earth. Nobody in the street will know their name.
They’ll be driven out of the light into darkness and chased out of the world.
They’ll have no son or grandson among their people, and no one will remain where they lived.
Those who come after will be stunned at what happened to them, just as those before were terrified.
That’s what happens to the homes of the unrighteous. That’s the place of someone who doesn’t know God.”
Then Job answered:
“How long are you going to torment me and crush me with your words?
Ten times now you’ve heaped insults on me. You’re not even ashamed to attack me.
Even if I really have gone wrong, that wrong is mine to carry.
If you’re set on making yourselves look bigger than me and using my disgrace as evidence against me,
then understand this: God has brought me down and closed his net around me.
“Look, I cry out, ‘I’ve been wronged!’ and nobody hears me. I call for help, and there’s no justice.
He’s walled off my road so I can’t get through. He’s put darkness on every path I take.
He’s stripped away my honor and taken the crown off my head.
He’s torn me down on every side, and I’m done for. He’s yanked up my hope like a tree.
He’s lit the fire of his anger against me and counts me as one of his enemies.
His troops come at me together, build a siege ramp against me, and camp all around my tent.
“He’s driven my brothers far from me. The people I used to know want nothing to do with me.
My relatives have gone away, and my close friends have forgotten me.
The people staying in my house and the women who serve there treat me like a stranger. I’m a foreigner to them.
I call my servant, and he doesn’t answer. I have to beg him myself.
My breath disgusts my wife. Even the children of my own mother can’t stand me.
Even little kids look down on me. When I get up, they talk against me.
All my close friends are disgusted with me. The people I loved have turned against me.
My bones stick to my skin and flesh. I’ve escaped by the skin of my teeth.
“Have pity on me! Have pity on me, my friends! God’s hand has touched me.
Why are you coming after me the way God does? Haven’t you had enough of my flesh?
“If only someone would write down my words! If only they were inscribed in a book!
If only they were carved into rock forever with an iron pen and lead!
But I know my Redeemer lives. In the end, he’ll stand on the earth.
After my skin is destroyed, I’ll see God in my flesh.
I’ll see him myself, on my side. I’ll see him with my own eyes, as someone I know. “My heart is worn out within me.
If you say, ‘We’re going to go after him,’ because you think I’m the root of the problem,
then be afraid of the sword. Anger brings punishment by the sword, and you’ll know there’s a judgment.”
Then Zophar the Naamathite answered:
“That’s why my thoughts are pushing me to answer. I feel the rush to speak.
I’ve heard the rebuke meant to shame me, and my own understanding gives me an answer.
Haven’t you known this from way back, ever since people were put on the earth?
The wicked don’t get to celebrate for long. The joy of the godless lasts a moment.
Even if their greatness climbs to heaven and their head reaches the clouds,
they’ll be gone for good like their own dung. People who saw them will ask, ‘Where’d they go?’
They’ll disappear like a dream, and nobody will find them. They’ll be chased away like a vision in the night.
The eyes that saw them won’t see them again. Even the place they lived won’t see them anymore.
Their children will have to seek the favor of the poor, and their own hands will give back their wealth.
Their bones are full of youthful strength, but that youth will lie down with them in the dust.
“Wickedness may taste sweet in their mouth, and they may hide it under their tongue.
They may savor it and refuse to let it go, keeping it in their mouth.
But once that food reaches their stomach, it turns into cobra venom inside them.
They swallowed riches, but they’ll throw them back up. God will drive those riches out of their belly.
They’ll suck in cobra venom. The viper’s tongue will kill them.
They won’t see rivers or flowing streams of honey and butter.
They’ll give back what they worked for without getting to swallow it down. They won’t enjoy the wealth they’ve gained.
They crushed the poor and left them behind. They seized a house by force and won’t build it up.
“Because they never knew peace inside, they won’t save a thing they took pleasure in.
There was nothing they didn’t gobble up, so their prosperity won’t last.
When they have more than enough, distress will catch up with them. Everyone who’s suffering will turn against them.
Just as they’re about to fill their belly, God will throw his fierce anger at them. It’ll rain down on them while they eat.
They’ll run from the iron weapon, only to be struck through by a bronze arrow.
They pull it out, and it comes out of their body, its shining point drawn from their liver. Terror comes over them.
Total darkness is waiting for their treasures. A fire no one fanned will devour them and burn up whatever’s left in their tent.
The heavens will expose their wrongdoing, and the earth will rise up against them.
The wealth of their household will be swept away, rushing off on the day of God’s anger.
That’s the share God gives the wicked, the inheritance he’s set aside for them.”
Then Job answered:
“Listen closely to what I’m saying. Let that be how you comfort me.
Give me a chance to speak. Once I’ve said my piece, go ahead and mock me.
Am I bringing my complaint to a human being? Why wouldn’t I be impatient?
Take a look at me and be stunned. Put your hand over your mouth.
When I remember it, I’m shaken. My whole body shudders in horror.
“Why do the wicked go on living, grow old, and even get more powerful?
Their children are settled right there with them, their descendants in front of their own eyes.
Their homes are safe from fear, and God’s rod doesn’t come down on them.
Their bulls breed without fail, and their cows give birth without miscarrying.
They send their little ones out like a flock, and their children dance.
They sing to the tambourine and harp and celebrate to the sound of the pipe.
They spend their days doing well, then go down to Sheol in an instant.
They tell God, ‘Leave us alone. We don’t want to know your ways.
Who is the Almighty that we should serve him? What would we get out of praying to him?’
Look, their prosperity isn’t in their own hands. I want nothing to do with the advice of the wicked.
“How often does the lamp of the wicked actually go out? How often does disaster come crashing down on them? How often does God hand out grief in his anger?
How often are they like stubble blown by the wind, like chaff a storm sweeps away?
You say, ‘God saves up the punishment for their children.’ Let him pay the person back directly so they know it themselves.
Let them see their own destruction with their own eyes. Let them drink the anger of the Almighty.
What do they care about the family they leave behind once their months have been cut short?
“Can anyone teach God anything, when he judges even those who are high up?
One person dies in full strength, completely at ease and undisturbed.
Their milk pails are full, and the marrow in their bones is still moist.
Another dies bitter at heart and never gets a taste of anything good.
Both lie down in the same dust, and worms cover them.
“Look, I know what you’re thinking and what you’re plotting to do to wrong me.
You ask, ‘Where’s the ruler’s house now? Where’s the tent the wicked used to live in?’
Haven’t you asked people who’ve traveled? Don’t you know what they can tell you,
that the wicked are kept for the day of disaster and led out to the day of wrath?
Who calls them out to their face for the way they’ve lived? Who pays them back for what they’ve done?
Yet they’ll be carried to the grave, and people will keep watch over their tomb.
The clumps of earth in the valley will be sweet to them. People will follow after them, just as countless others went before them.
So how do you expect to comfort me with nonsense? There’s nothing left in your answers but lies.”
Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered:
“Can a person do anything that benefits God? A wise person’s wisdom helps them.
Does the Almighty take any pleasure in you being in the right? Does he gain anything if you live without fault?
Is it because you honor God that he corrects you and takes you to court?
Isn’t your wickedness huge? There’s no end to the wrong you’ve done.
You took collateral from your own brother for no reason, and you stripped the clothes off people who had nothing.
You gave no water to those worn out with thirst, and you held back bread from the hungry.
But the powerful man got the land, and the man everyone honored got to live in it.
You sent widows away with empty hands, and the arms of the fatherless were broken.
That’s why traps are all around you and sudden terror shakes you,
or darkness keeps you from seeing and floodwaters cover you.
“Isn’t God high in heaven? Look how far up the stars are!
You say, ‘What does God know? Can he judge through all that darkness?
Thick clouds hide things from him so he can’t see. He walks along the vault of the sky.’
Are you going to stick to the old road wicked people walked?
They were swept away before their time. Their foundation washed away like a stream.
They told God, ‘Leave us alone!’ and asked, ‘What can the Almighty do for us?’
Yet he filled their houses with good things. I want nothing to do with the advice of the wicked.
The righteous see it and are glad, and the innocent laugh at them,
saying, ‘The ones who rose against us have been cut off. Fire has burned up what was left of them.’
“Get to know God now, and be at peace. Good will come to you that way.
Please take in what he teaches you and keep his words in your heart.
If you return to the Almighty and put wrongdoing far away from your tents, you’ll be built back up.
Put your treasure in the dust and your gold from Ophir among the stones in the streams.
Then the Almighty will be your treasure, your precious silver.
Then you’ll find joy in the Almighty and lift your face to God.
You’ll pray to him, and he’ll hear you. You’ll keep the vows you made.
You’ll decide on something, and it’ll be established for you. Light will shine on your paths.
When people bring you down, you’ll say, ‘Be lifted up.’ God will save the humble person.
He’ll even rescue someone who isn’t innocent. Yes, they’ll be rescued because your hands are clean.”
Then Job answered:
“Even today my complaint is defiant. His hand still weighs heavy on me, even though I’m groaning.
If only I knew where to find him! If only I could get all the way to his seat!
I’d lay out my case before him and have every argument ready to say.
I’d hear how he’d answer me and understand what he had to tell me.
Would he use all his power to argue against me? No, he’d listen to me.
There an upright person could reason with him, and I’d be free from my judge for good.
“If I go east, he isn’t there. If I go west, I can’t find him.
He’s at work in the north, but I can’t see him. He turns south, but I can’t catch even a glimpse of him.
But he knows the road I’m on. When he’s tested me, I’ll come out like gold.
My feet have stayed in his steps. I’ve kept to his road and haven’t turned away.
I haven’t backed away from what he commanded. I’ve treasured the words he spoke more than the food I need.
But he stands alone. Who can stand against him? Whatever he wants to do, he does.
He carries out what he’s appointed for me, and he has many things like that in store.
That’s why I’m terrified in his presence. When I think it through, I’m afraid of him.
God has made my heart faint. The Almighty has terrified me.
I wasn’t cut off before the darkness came, and he didn’t hide the thick darkness from my face.
“Why doesn’t the Almighty set times for judgment? Why don’t those who know him get to see his days?
Some people move the boundary markers. They seize flocks by force and feed them as their own.
They drive off the donkey of a fatherless child and take a widow’s ox as collateral.
They shove the needy out of the way, and the poor of the land all go into hiding.
Look at them, out working like wild donkeys in the desert, searching hard for food. The wilderness gives them something to feed their children.
They cut what food they can in the fields and pick what’s left in the vineyard of the wicked.
They spend the whole night without clothes, with nothing to cover them in the cold.
Mountain rains soak them. With nowhere to shelter, they cling to the rock.
Some people snatch a fatherless child away from the breast and take collateral from the poor.
So the poor go around naked, with nothing to wear. They carry bundles of grain while they’re hungry themselves.
They press oil inside those people’s walls. They tread the winepresses while they go thirsty.
People groan from the crowded city, and the wounded cry out from deep inside. Yet God pays no attention to the wrong.
“These are the ones who rebel against the light. They don’t know its ways or stay on its paths.
The murderer gets up at first light and kills the poor and needy. At night he acts like a thief.
The adulterer watches for twilight, thinking, ‘Nobody will see me.’ Then he disguises his face.
In the dark they dig through the walls of houses. In the daytime they shut themselves in. They don’t know the light.
Morning is like thick darkness to all of them, because they know the terrors of deep darkness.
“They’re like foam on the water. Their share of the land is cursed, and they don’t take the road into the vineyards.
Drought and heat swallow up meltwater. That’s how Sheol swallows those who’ve sinned.
Even the womb that bore them will forget them. Worms will feast on them, and nobody will remember them anymore. Wrongdoing will be broken like a tree.
They prey on the woman who has no children and show no kindness to the widow.
Yet God uses his power to keep the mighty alive. Even the one who can’t count on living gets back up.
God gives them security, and they settle into it. His eyes are on the way they live.
They’re lifted up, and a little while later they’re gone. They’re brought low and taken away like everyone else, cut off like heads of grain.
If that’s not how it is, who’ll prove me a liar and show that my words are worth nothing?”
Then Bildad the Shuhite answered:
“Rule and awe belong to God. He makes peace in his high places.
Can anyone count his armies? Is there anyone his light doesn’t rise on?
So how can a person be in the right before God? How can anyone born of a woman be clean?
Look, even the moon has no brightness, and even the stars aren’t pure in his sight.
How much less a human being, just a worm, a human child who’s no more than a worm!”
Then Job answered:
“What a help you’ve been to someone with no power! What a rescue for an arm with no strength!
What advice you’ve given to someone with no wisdom! You’ve poured out so much sound knowledge!
Who were you speaking to? Whose spirit spoke through you?
“The spirits of the dead tremble beneath the waters, along with all who live there.
Sheol lies bare before God. Nothing covers Abaddon.
He stretches the north over empty space and hangs the earth on nothing.
He wraps water up in thick clouds, and the clouds don’t burst under its weight.
He covers the face of his throne and spreads his cloud over it.
He draws a boundary on the surface of the waters, where light and darkness meet.
The pillars of heaven shake, stunned at his rebuke.
By his power he stirs up the sea. By his understanding he strikes through Rahab.
By his Spirit the heavens are made beautiful. His hand pierced the swift serpent.
Look, we’ve only seen the edges of his ways. We hear barely a whisper of him. Who could understand the thunder of his power?”
Job picked up his speech again:
“As surely as God lives, the God who’s denied me justice, the Almighty who’s filled me with bitterness,
as long as there’s life in me and God’s breath is in my nostrils,
my lips won’t say what’s wrong, and my tongue won’t tell a lie.
There’s no way I’ll say you’re right. Until I die, I won’t give up my integrity.
I’m holding on to my righteousness, and I won’t let go. My heart won’t accuse me as long as I live.
“Let my enemy end up like the wicked. Let anyone who rises against me end up like the unrighteous.
What hope does a godless person have when they’re cut off, when God takes away their life?
Will God hear them cry when trouble comes for them?
Will they take joy in the Almighty? Will they call on God at all times?
I’ll teach you about God’s hand. I won’t hide what’s with the Almighty.
Look, you’ve all seen it yourselves. So why have you gotten caught up in such empty talk?
“Here’s the share a wicked person gets from God, the inheritance oppressors receive from the Almighty.
If they have lots of children, those children are headed for the sword. Their descendants won’t have enough bread to eat.
Death will bury those who survive them, and their widows won’t mourn.
They may pile up silver like dust and stack up clothes like heaps of clay.
They can stack those clothes all they want, but the righteous will wear them, and the innocent will divide up the silver.
They build a house like a moth’s shelter, like a watchman’s temporary hut.
They lie down rich, but they won’t do it again. They open their eyes, and they’re gone.
Terrors catch up to them like floodwaters. A storm snatches them away in the night.
The east wind carries them off, and away they go. It sweeps them right out of their place.
It hurls itself at them without mercy while they try to escape its grip.
People clap their hands at them and hiss them out of their place.”
“There’s a mine for silver and a place where people refine gold.
Iron comes out of the earth, and copper is smelted from ore.
People push back the darkness. They search to its farthest limits for stones deep in the dark.
They cut a shaft far from where people live, where no feet pass. Far from everyone, they hang there and swing back and forth.
Food comes up from the earth, but underneath, the ground is churned up as if by fire.
Its rocks yield sapphires, and its dust holds gold.
No bird of prey knows that path. Even a falcon’s eye hasn’t seen it.
Proud animals haven’t stepped there, and no fierce lion has passed that way.
People put their hands to flint and overturn mountains at the roots.
They cut channels through rock, and their eyes spot every precious thing.
They dam up streams so they don’t trickle through. They bring what’s hidden out into the light.
“But where do you find wisdom? Where does understanding live?
People don’t know its price, and you won’t find it in the land of the living.
The deep says, ‘It isn’t in me.’ The sea says, ‘It isn’t with me.’
You can’t buy it with gold or weigh out silver to pay for it.
You can’t put a price on it in gold from Ophir, precious onyx, or sapphire.
Gold and glass can’t match it. You can’t trade fine gold jewelry for it.
Coral and crystal aren’t even worth bringing up. Wisdom is worth more than rubies.
Topaz from Ethiopia can’t match it, and pure gold can’t measure its worth.
So where does wisdom come from? Where does understanding live?
It’s hidden from the eyes of every living thing, even from the birds in the sky.
Destruction and Death say, ‘We’ve heard a rumor about it.’
“God knows the way to wisdom, and he knows where it lives.
He looks to the ends of the earth and sees everything under the sky.
He set the strength of the wind and measured out the waters.
When he made a decree for the rain and laid out a path for the lightning that comes with thunder,
he saw wisdom and made it known. He established it and searched it out.
He told humanity, ‘Look, wisdom is fearing the Lord. Understanding is turning away from evil.’”
Job picked up his speech again:
“If only I could go back to those earlier months, to the days when God watched over me,
when his lamp shone over my head and I could walk through darkness by his light.
I was in my prime then, and God’s friendship was there in my tent.
The Almighty was still with me, and all my children were around me.
My steps were bathed in butter, and the rock poured out streams of oil for me.
I’d go out to the city gate and take my seat in the public square.
Young men would see me and step out of sight. The elders would get to their feet and stand.
The leaders would stop talking and put a hand over their mouths.
The nobles’ voices would go quiet. Their tongues would stick to the roofs of their mouths.
People who heard me blessed me, and people who saw me spoke well of me,
because I rescued the poor who cried out and the fatherless who had nobody to help them.
Those who were about to die blessed me, and I made the widow’s heart sing for joy.
I put on righteousness like clothing. Justice was my robe and my crown.
I was eyes for people who couldn’t see and feet for people who couldn’t walk.
I was a father to those in need. I looked into the case of someone I didn’t even know.
I broke the jaws of the unjust and pulled their prey right out of their teeth.
Then I thought, ‘I’ll die in my own home. My days will be as many as grains of sand.
My roots reach out to the water, and dew rests on my branches all night.
My honor stays fresh, and my bow is renewed in my hand.’
“People listened and waited for me. They stayed quiet to hear my advice.
When I finished speaking, nobody spoke again. My words settled over them.
They waited for me the way people wait for rain. They drank in my words like spring rain.
When they’d lost confidence, I smiled at them. They didn’t turn away from the light of my face.
I chose the way for them and sat as their leader. I lived like a king among his troops, like someone who comforts people in mourning.
“But now people younger than me laugh at me, people whose fathers I thought weren’t fit to be put with my sheepdogs.
What good was the strength of their hands to me, when their strength had already gone?
They’re gaunt from hunger and famine. They gnaw at the dry ground in the gloom of the desolate wasteland.
They pull up salt herbs by the bushes and eat the roots of the broom tree.
People drive them out and shout after them as if they were thieves,
so they live in dreadful valleys and in holes in the ground and the rocks.
They bray among the bushes and huddle together under the nettles.
They’re children of fools, children of wicked people. They were whipped out of the land.
“Now I’m the subject of their songs. My name has become a joke to them.
They can’t stand me. They keep their distance and don’t hesitate to spit in my face.
God has loosened his cord and afflicted me, and they’ve thrown off all restraint in front of me.
The rabble rises up on my right. They knock my feet out from under me and build up paths to destroy me.
They tear up my path and push on with my destruction without anyone helping them.
They pour through as if through a wide gap in a wall, rolling in through the ruins.
Terrors have turned on me. They chase my honor away like the wind, and my well-being has vanished like a cloud.
“Now my soul is pouring out inside me. Days of suffering have got hold of me.
At night my bones feel pierced, and the pain that gnaws at me never lets up.
My clothes are pulled out of shape by sheer force. They grip me like the collar of my tunic.
He’s thrown me into the mud. I’ve become like dust and ashes.
I cry out to you, and you don’t answer. I stand up, and you just stare at me.
You’ve turned cruel toward me. You come after me with the full strength of your hand.
You lift me into the wind and drive me along with it. You dissolve me in the storm.
I know you’ll bring me to death, to the house set aside for everyone who lives.
“Doesn’t a person stretch out a hand when they fall? Don’t they cry for help when disaster hits?
Didn’t I cry for people in trouble? Didn’t I grieve deep down for those in need?
I looked for good, and evil came. I waited for light, and darkness came.
My heart churns and won’t rest. Days of suffering have come upon me.
I go around mourning without the sun. I stand up in the gathering and cry for help.
I’m a brother to jackals and a companion to ostriches.
My skin turns black and peels off. My bones burn with heat.
So my harp has turned to mourning, and my pipe sounds like people weeping.
“I made a covenant with my eyes. How could I look at a young woman with lust?
What share would I get from God above? What inheritance would the Almighty on high give me?
Isn’t it calamity for the unrighteous and disaster for people who do wrong?
Doesn’t he see how I live and count every step I take?
“If I’ve walked with lies and rushed into deceit,
then weigh me on honest scales so God can know my integrity.
If I’ve stepped off the right path, if my heart has chased what my eyes saw, or if any stain has stuck to my hands,
then let me plant and someone else eat. Let what grows in my field be pulled up by the roots.
“If my heart has been drawn to another woman and I’ve lain in wait at my neighbor’s door,
then let my wife grind grain for another man and let others sleep with her.
That would be a terrible crime, a wrong for the judges to punish.
It’s a fire that burns all the way to destruction and would uproot everything I’ve gained.
“If I brushed aside the complaint of a man or woman who serves me when they had a case against me,
what would I do when God rises up? When he calls me to account, what would I say?
Didn’t the same one who made me in the womb make my servant too? Didn’t one God shape us both in the womb?
“If I’ve refused the poor what they needed or let a widow’s eyes fail from waiting,
or eaten my own bit of food alone without sharing it with the fatherless,
though from my youth I’ve raised the fatherless like a father, and from my earliest days I’ve guided the widow,
if I’ve watched someone perish for lack of clothes or seen a needy person with nothing to cover them,
if their heart hasn’t blessed me because wool from my own sheep kept them warm,
if I’ve raised my hand against the fatherless because I knew I had support at the city gate,
then let my shoulder fall from its blade and my arm break off at the bone.
Disaster from God terrifies me. Before his majesty I can do nothing.
“If I’ve put my hope in gold and told fine gold, ‘You’re what I count on,’
if I’ve celebrated how rich I was and how much my own hand had gained,
if I’ve watched the sun shining or the moon moving in splendor,
and my heart got drawn in secretly and I blew them a kiss from my hand,
that too would be a wrong for the judges to punish. I’d have denied God above.
“If I’ve celebrated the downfall of someone who hated me or felt triumphant when trouble caught up with them,
though I’ve never let my mouth sin by calling down a curse on their life,
if the men of my household haven’t said, ‘Who can find anyone who hasn’t eaten their fill of his meat?’
though no foreigner had to spend the night in the street because I opened my doors to travelers,
if I’ve covered up my wrongs like Adam, hiding my guilt in my heart,
because I feared the crowd and was so scared of being looked down on by families that I kept quiet and stayed indoors,
if only I had someone who’d hear me! Look, here’s my signature! Let the Almighty answer me! Let my accuser write out the charges!
I’d carry them on my shoulder and wear them like a crown.
I’d tell him every step I took. I’d approach him like a prince.
If my land cries out against me and its furrows weep together,
if I’ve eaten what it grew without paying or caused its owners to lose their lives,
then let thorns grow instead of wheat and stinkweed instead of barley.” That’s the end of Job’s words.
The three men stopped answering Job because he was right in his own eyes.
Then Elihu son of Barachel the Buzite, from the family of Ram, got angry at Job for putting himself in the right over God.
He was angry at Job’s three friends too. They hadn’t found an answer, yet they’d condemned Job anyway.
Elihu had waited to speak to Job because the others were older than he was.
But when he saw that none of those three men had an answer, his anger flared up.
Elihu son of Barachel the Buzite answered, “I’m young, and you’re very old. So I held back and didn’t dare tell you what I thought.
I thought, ‘Let age have its say. People who’ve lived many years should teach wisdom.’
But there’s a spirit in people, and the Spirit of the Almighty gives them understanding.
Being important doesn’t make people wise, and being old doesn’t mean they know what’s just.
So I said, ‘Listen to me. I’ll tell you what I think too.’
“Look, I waited for you to speak and listened to your reasoning while you worked out what to say.
I gave you my full attention, but none of you convinced Job or answered what he said.
Don’t go saying, ‘We’ve found wisdom. God can prove him wrong. No human can.’
Job hasn’t aimed his words at me, and I won’t answer him with your arguments.
“They’re stunned. They’ve stopped answering. They don’t have a word left to say.
Should I keep waiting while they stand there in silence with nothing more to say?
I’ll give my own answer. I’ll tell you what I think too.
I’ve got so much to say. The spirit inside me won’t let me hold it back.
My chest is like wine with no way to vent, like new wineskins about to burst.
I’ll speak so I can get some relief. I’ll open my mouth and answer.
Please, let me show no favoritism or give anyone a flattering title.
I don’t know how to flatter people. If I did, my Maker would soon take me away.
“Job, please hear me out. Listen to everything I have to say.
Look, I’ve opened my mouth. My tongue is already speaking.
What I say comes from an honest heart. I’ll speak sincerely about what I know.
God’s Spirit made me. The breath of the Almighty keeps me alive.
If you can answer me, go ahead. Get your words in order and stand up to face me.
Look, before God I stand where you do. I was shaped out of clay too.
You don’t have to be afraid of me, and I won’t weigh you down with pressure.
“I heard what you said. I heard you say it myself:
‘I’m clean and haven’t disobeyed. I’m innocent. There’s no wrongdoing in me.
Look, God finds reasons to accuse me. He counts me as his enemy.
He locks my feet in the stocks. He keeps track of every path I take.’
“Here’s my answer. You aren’t in the right about this, because God is greater than any human being.
Why argue with him because he doesn’t explain everything he does?
God speaks once, even twice, though people pay no attention.
In a dream, in a vision at night, when deep sleep comes over people as they lie in bed,
he opens their ears and seals the instruction he gives them,
to turn them away from what they planned and keep them from pride.
He holds them back from the pit and keeps them from dying by the sword.
“A person also gets corrected through pain in bed, with a struggle in their bones that won’t let up,
until they can’t stand bread or even the finest food.
Their flesh wastes away until you can hardly see it. Bones you couldn’t see before now stick out.
They’re nearing the pit, and their life is drawing close to the destroyers.
“If there’s an angel at their side, an interpreter, one out of a thousand, to show them what’s right for them,
then God is gracious to them and says, ‘Rescue them from going down to the pit. I’ve found a ransom.’
Their flesh will be fresher than a child’s. They’ll get back the vigor of their youth.
They’ll pray to God, and he’ll look on them with favor. They’ll see his face with joy, and he’ll restore their righteousness.
They’ll sing in front of others and say, ‘I sinned and twisted what was right, and it did me no good.
He bought me back from going into the pit. My life will see the light.’
“Look, God does all these things for a person twice, even three times,
to bring them back from the pit so they can see the light of the living again.
Pay close attention, Job. Listen to me. Stay quiet for a moment, and I’ll speak.
If you have something to say, answer me. Speak up, because I want to show that you’re in the right.
If you have nothing to say, listen to me. Stay quiet, and I’ll teach you wisdom.”
Elihu went on:
“Listen to what I’m saying, you wise people. Hear me out, you who have knowledge.
The ear tests words the way your mouth tastes food.
Let’s work out what’s right and figure out together what’s good.
Job has said, ‘I’m in the right, and God has taken away my right.
Even though I’m in the right, I’m treated like a liar. My wound won’t heal, though I haven’t disobeyed.’
Who’s like Job, who drinks scorn like water,
who keeps company with people who do wrong and walks with the wicked?
He’s said, ‘A person gains nothing by taking delight in God.’
“So listen to me, you people who understand. Far be it from God to do evil or from the Almighty to do wrong.
He pays people back for what they do. He lets each person find what their own way of living brings.
God will never do evil. The Almighty won’t twist justice.
Who put him in charge of the earth? Who appointed him over the whole world?
If he set his heart on himself and gathered his spirit and breath back to himself,
all living flesh would die together, and humanity would turn back to dust.
“If you understand, hear this. Listen to what I’m saying.
Should someone who hates justice be in charge? Would you condemn the one who’s righteous and mighty,
the one who can tell a king, ‘You’re vile!’ and tell nobles, ‘You’re wicked!’?
He plays no favorites with rulers and gives the rich no more respect than the poor. His hands made them all.
In a moment they die, even at midnight. People are shaken and pass away, and the mighty are taken out of the way without a hand touching them.
“His eyes are on the way people live. He sees every step they take.
There’s no darkness or deep gloom where people who do wrong can hide.
He doesn’t need to look into a person any further before they come before him in judgment.
He shatters the mighty in ways we can’t figure out and puts others in their place.
He knows what they’ve done. He overturns them in the night, and they’re destroyed.
He strikes them as evildoers where everyone can see,
because they turned away from following him and wouldn’t pay attention to any of his ways.
They made the poor cry out to him, and he heard the cry of those who were suffering.
When he gives quiet, who can condemn? When he hides his face, who can see him? He’s over a nation and an individual alike,
so the godless don’t rule and nobody can trap the people.
“Has anyone said to God, ‘I’m guilty, but I won’t do wrong anymore.
Teach me what I can’t see. If I’ve done wrong, I won’t do it again’?
Should God pay you back on your terms because you reject his decision? You have to choose, not me. So tell us what you know.
People with understanding will tell me this, and so will every wise person who hears me:
‘Job speaks without knowledge. There’s no wisdom in his words.’
I wish Job were put to the test all the way to the end, because he answers like wicked people do.
He piles rebellion on top of his sin. He claps his hands among us and keeps adding words against God.”
Elihu went on:
“Do you think you’re in the right? Are you saying, ‘I’m more righteous than God,’
when you ask, ‘What advantage is it to you? What do I gain over what I’d have gained if I’d sinned?’
I’ll answer you and your friends too.
Look up at the skies. See how high the clouds are above you.
If you sin, what does that do to him? If you pile up offenses, what have you done to him?
If you’re righteous, what have you given him? What does he get from your hand?
Your wickedness can hurt somebody like you, and your righteousness can help another human being.
“People cry out under so much oppression. They call for help against the arm of the powerful.
But nobody says, ‘Where’s God my Maker, who gives songs in the night,
who teaches us more than the animals on earth and makes us wiser than the birds in the sky?’
They cry out, but no one answers because of the arrogance of evil people.
God won’t listen to an empty cry. The Almighty won’t pay attention to it.
How much less when you say you can’t see him! Your case is before him, so wait for him.
But now, because he hasn’t come in anger and doesn’t pay much attention to arrogance,
Job opens his mouth with empty talk and piles up words without knowing what he’s talking about.”
Elihu kept speaking:
“Bear with me a little longer, and I’ll show you. I still have something to say on God’s behalf.
I’ll draw on knowledge from far away and give my Maker credit for what’s right.
I’m telling you the truth. Someone with complete knowledge is here with you.
“Look, God is mighty, yet he looks down on no one. His understanding is mighty too.
He doesn’t keep the wicked alive, but he gives justice to those who suffer.
He keeps his eyes on the righteous. He seats them with kings on the throne, where they’re lifted up forever.
If they’re bound in shackles and caught in the ropes of suffering,
he shows them what they’ve done and how they’ve done wrong by acting proudly.
He opens their ears to correction and tells them to turn back from wrongdoing.
If they listen and serve him, they’ll spend their days doing well and their years in enjoyment.
But if they refuse to listen, they’ll die by the sword. They’ll die without understanding.
“People who are godless at heart store up anger. They don’t cry for help when he binds them.
They die young, and their lives end among the unclean.
He rescues people through the very suffering they endure. He opens their ears through oppression.
He would’ve drawn you out of distress into a wide-open place with nothing hemming you in. Your table would’ve been loaded with rich food.
“But you’re full of the judgment that falls on the wicked. Judgment and justice have a grip on you.
Don’t let riches lure you into anger. Don’t let even a huge bribe turn you aside.
Could your wealth keep you going in distress? Could all your strength do it?
Don’t long for the night, when people are cut off right where they are.
Watch yourself. Don’t turn to wrongdoing. You’ve chosen it over suffering.
Look how high God stands in his power. Who teaches like him?
Who’s ever told him what path to take? Who can say to him, ‘You’ve done wrong’?
“Remember to praise his work, the work people sing about.
Everyone has looked at it. People see it from far away.
Look, God is great, beyond what we know. No one can count his years.
He draws the water up in drops, and the vapor condenses into rain.
The skies pour it out, and it falls on people in abundance.
Can anyone make sense of how the clouds spread or how thunder rolls from his shelter?
Look, he spreads his light all around him and covers the bottom of the sea.
With these things he judges the peoples and gives them plenty of food.
He wraps his hands in lightning and commands it to hit its mark.
The thunder tells of him, and even the livestock know a storm is coming.
“At this my heart shakes and jumps out of its place.
Listen, really listen, to the roar of his voice, the sound coming from his mouth.
He sends it out under the whole sky and sends his lightning to the ends of the earth.
After the lightning, his voice roars. He thunders with his majestic voice and holds nothing back when he’s heard.
God thunders in a way that leaves us amazed. He does great things we can’t understand.
He tells the snow, ‘Fall on the earth,’ and gives the same command to the rain, even the heaviest downpours.
He puts a stop to the work of every hand so that all the people he made can recognize what he’s doing.
Then the animals take cover and stay in their dens.
The storm comes out from its room, and cold comes down from the north.
God breathes, and ice forms. The wide waters freeze over.
He loads the thick clouds with moisture and spreads out his lightning clouds.
They turn wherever he guides them to do whatever he commands across the inhabited earth.
He sends them to correct people, to water his land, or to show his faithful love.
“Listen to this, Job. Stand still and think about the amazing things God does.
Do you know how he directs them or makes lightning flash from his cloud?
Do you know how the clouds work, the wonders of the one whose knowledge is perfect?
You’re the one whose clothes get hot when the south wind leaves the earth still.
Can you help him spread out the sky, hard as a mirror made of cast metal?
Teach us what to say to him. We can’t lay out our case in the dark.
Should he be told I want to speak? Would anyone ask to be swallowed up?
People can’t see the bright light in the sky until the wind comes through and clears it.
Golden splendor comes out of the north. God is surrounded by awesome majesty.
We can’t reach the Almighty. His power is high above us. With all his justice and righteousness, he won’t oppress anyone.
That’s why people revere him. He pays no attention to those who are wise in their own hearts.”
Then the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind:
“Who is this clouding good counsel with words they don’t understand?
Brace yourself like a man. I’ll ask the questions, and you’ll answer me.
“Where were you when I laid the earth’s foundations? Tell me, if you understand.
Who set its dimensions? Surely you know. Who stretched the measuring line across it?
What held its foundations in place? Who set its cornerstone
while the morning stars sang together and all God’s sons shouted for joy?
“Who shut the sea behind doors when it burst out of the womb,
when I dressed it in clouds and wrapped it in thick darkness,
when I marked out its boundary and put bars and doors in place,
and said, ‘You can come this far and no farther. Your proud waves stop here’?
“Have you ever given the morning an order or shown the dawn where it belongs,
so it could grab the edges of the earth and shake the wicked out of it?
The earth takes shape like clay under a seal, and its features stand out like a garment.
The wicked lose their light, and the arm raised high is broken.
“Have you gone down to the springs of the sea? Have you walked through the hidden places of the deep?
Have the gates of death been shown to you? Have you seen the gates of death’s shadow?
Have you taken in how wide the earth is? Speak up if you know it all.
“Which road leads to where light lives? And where does darkness stay?
Can you take it to its boundary? Do you know the paths to its home?
Of course you know. You were already born back then, and you’ve lived so many days!
Have you been inside the storehouses of snow or seen where the hail is stored,
the hail I’ve kept for times of trouble, for the day of battle and war?
Which way does lightning spread out? How does the east wind scatter across the earth?
Who cut a channel for floodwater and made a path for the thunderstorm,
so rain falls on land where nobody lives, on wilderness with no one in it,
so it can soak that empty, desolate ground and make tender grass grow?
Does the rain have a father? Who fathered the drops of dew?
Whose womb did ice come from? Who gave birth to the gray frost from the sky?
