The waters turn hard as stone when the surface of the deep freezes over.
“Can you tie together the cluster of the Pleiades or untie Orion’s cords?
Can you bring the constellations out in their season? Can you guide the Bear and her cubs?
Do you know the laws of the heavens? Can you set their rule over the earth?
“Can you shout to the clouds and have a flood of water cover you?
Can you send lightning bolts on their way? Do they report back to you, ‘Here we are’?
Who put wisdom deep within? Who gave the mind understanding?
Who’s wise enough to count the clouds? Who can tip over the jars of the sky
when the dust clumps up and the lumps of earth stick together?
“Can you hunt prey for the lioness or feed the young lions until they’re full,
while they crouch in their dens and wait in the thicket?
Who gets food for the raven when its young cry out to God and wander around with nothing to eat?
“Do you know when mountain goats give birth? Do you watch the doe have her fawns?
Can you count the months they carry their young? Do you know when they’ll give birth?
They crouch down, deliver their young, and are done with the pain of labor.
Their little ones get strong out in the open fields. They leave and don’t come back.
“Who let the wild donkey go free? Who untied the swift donkey,
the one I gave the wilderness for a home and the salt lands to live in?
It scoffs at the city’s racket. It can’t hear a driver shouting orders.
The mountain range is its pasture. It looks for anything green to eat.
“Will the wild ox be happy to work for you? Will it stay by your feeding trough?
Can you keep a wild ox in the furrow with a harness? Will it follow you and plow the valleys?
Will you trust it because it’s so strong? Will you leave your work to it?
Can you count on it to bring your seed home and gather the grain from your threshing floor?
“The ostrich flaps her wings proudly, but are those feathers and plumes full of love?
She leaves her eggs on the ground and warms them in the dust.
She forgets a foot could crush them or a wild animal could trample them.
She treats her young harshly, like they aren’t even hers. She isn’t afraid her work might all be for nothing,
because God kept wisdom from her and didn’t give her understanding.
But when she lifts herself up, she scoffs at the horse and its rider.
“Did you give the horse its strength? Did you dress its neck with a shaking mane?
Did you make it leap like a locust? Its mighty snort is something to hear.
It paws the ground in the valley and delights in its strength. It charges out to meet armed men.
It laughs at fear and doesn’t get rattled. It won’t turn back from the sword.
The quiver rattles against it, along with the flashing spear and javelin.
It eats up the ground in fierce rage. When the trumpet sounds, it won’t stand still.
Every time the trumpet blows, it snorts, ‘Aha!’ It smells the battle from far away, the thunder of commanders and all the shouting.
“Is it your wisdom that makes the hawk soar and spread her wings toward the south?
Is it your order that sends the eagle up to build its nest high above?
It lives on the cliff, making its home on the rocky point, in its stronghold.
From there it scouts for prey. Its eyes spot it from far away.
Its young suck up blood. Wherever the slain are, there it is.”
Then the LORD answered Job again:
“Is the one who argues going to take on the Almighty? Let the one who challenges God answer.”
Job answered the LORD:
“Look, I’m of little account. What could I say back to you? I put my hand over my mouth.
I’ve spoken once, and I won’t answer again. Twice, even, but I won’t say another word.”
Then the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind:
“Brace yourself like a man. I’ll ask the questions, and you’ll answer me.
Are you going to overturn my judgment? Are you going to condemn me so you can be in the right?
Do you have an arm as strong as God’s? Can your voice thunder like his?
“Go on, dress yourself in greatness and dignity. Put on honor and majesty.
Pour out the fury of your anger. Look at everyone who’s proud and bring them low.
Look at every proud person and humble them. Crush the wicked right where they stand.
Hide them all together in the dust. Bind their faces in that hidden place.
Then I’ll admit to you that your own right hand can save you.
“Look at Behemoth. I made him just as I made you. He eats grass like an ox.
Look at the strength in his thighs, the power in the muscles of his belly.
He moves his tail like a cedar. The sinews of his thighs are woven together.
His bones are like bronze tubes. His limbs are like iron bars.
He’s foremost among God’s works. The one who made him gives him his sword.
The mountains grow food for him, where all the animals of the field play.
He lies under lotus trees, hidden among the reeds in the marsh.
The lotus trees shade him, and willows by the stream surround him.
Look, even when a river floods, he doesn’t shake. He stays confident even if the Jordan rises right up to his mouth.
Can anyone catch him while he’s watching or pierce his nose with a snare?
“Can you pull Leviathan out with a fishhook or tie down his tongue with a cord?
Can you put a rope through his nose or drive a hook through his jaw?
Will he beg you over and over? Will he speak gently to you?
Will he make a deal with you to be your servant forever?
Will you play with him like a bird or tie him up for your girls?
Will traders bargain for him and divide him among the merchants?
Can you fill his hide with barbed irons or his head with fishing spears?
Go ahead, lay a hand on him. You’ll remember the fight and never do it again.
Look, any hope of catching him is wasted. Won’t you fall down at the mere sight of him?
Nobody is fierce enough to stir him up. So who can stand in front of me?
Who’s ever given me anything first, so I owe them something back? Everything under heaven is mine.
“I won’t keep quiet about his limbs, his great strength, or his impressive build.
Who can strip off his outer covering? Who would go inside his jaws?
Who can pry open the doors of his face? His teeth are surrounded by terror.
His pride is his strong scales, locked together like a tight seal.
Each one fits so close to the next that no air gets between them.
They’re joined and stick together so tightly that they can’t be pulled apart.
When he sneezes, light flashes. His eyes are like the eyelids of dawn.
Burning torches shoot from his mouth. Sparks leap out.
Smoke pours from his nostrils like steam from a pot boiling over burning reeds.
His breath sets coals alight. Flames come out of his mouth.
Strength lives in his neck, and terror dances ahead of him.
The folds of his flesh are joined tight. They’re firm on him and won’t budge.
His heart is hard as stone, as hard as the lower millstone.
When he rises up, even the mighty get scared. They back away as he thrashes.
A sword can’t get the better of him, and neither can a spear, a dart, or a pointed shaft.
He treats iron like straw and bronze like rotten wood.
An arrow won’t make him run. Sling stones are like chaff to him.
Clubs are just stubble to him. He laughs when a javelin comes rushing at him.
His underside is like sharp pieces of pottery. He leaves tracks in the mud like a threshing sled.
He makes the deep boil like a pot and churns the sea like a pot of ointment.
He leaves a shining trail behind him. You’d think the deep had white hair.
Nothing on earth is his equal. He’s made without fear.
He looks on everything high and mighty. He’s king over all the sons of pride.”
Then Job answered the LORD:
“I know you can do anything, and nobody can stop what you’ve set out to do.
You asked, ‘Who’s this hiding counsel without knowledge?’ I spoke about things I didn’t understand, things too wonderful for me to know.
You said, ‘Listen now, and I’ll speak. I’ll ask you questions, and you’ll answer me.’
I’d heard about you with my ears, but now I see you with my own eyes.
So I’m disgusted with myself, and I repent in dust and ashes.”
After the LORD had spoken these words to Job, he told Eliphaz the Temanite, “I’m angry with you and your two friends. You haven’t spoken rightly about me the way my servant Job has.

So take seven bulls and seven rams and go to my servant Job. Offer a burnt offering for yourselves. My servant Job will pray for you, and I’ll accept him so I don’t deal with you as your foolishness deserves. You haven’t spoken rightly about me the way my servant Job has.”
So Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite went and did what the LORD told them. The LORD accepted Job.
The LORD restored Job’s prosperity when he prayed for his friends. The LORD gave Job twice what he’d had before.

All his brothers and sisters and everyone who’d known him before came and ate with him in his house. They comforted him over all the trouble the LORD had brought on him. Each gave him a piece of money and a gold ring.
The LORD blessed Job’s later years more than his beginning. Job had 14,000 sheep, 6,000 camels, 1,000 pairs of oxen, and 1,000 female donkeys.
He also had seven sons and three daughters.
He named the first daughter Jemimah, the second Keziah, and the third Keren Happuch.
Nowhere in the land were there women as beautiful as Job’s daughters. Their father gave them an inheritance alongside their brothers.
After that, Job lived 140 years and saw his children and their children down to four generations.
Then Job died, old and full of days.
